That can erase the frequency patterns that distinguish one fault from another, especially across different resolutions.
863.ap: Fed-S2's core move is to stop treating shared model parameters as the thing that must travel between sites. Each site turns its local multimodal sensor evidence into a lighter semantic description, meaning a compressed numerical description intended to preserve fault-relevant meaning rather than raw readings. Before sharing, that description is sanitized by Semantic-Shielding, which is presented as a way to hide private reconstructable detail while keeping diagnostic signal. The server then constructs a global knowledge graph, a map whose nodes are these descriptions and whose links organize related fault evidence across sites. When a new case arrives, the system retrieves nearby or relevant pieces from this graph and gives them to a frozen Meta Llama-3.1 model for cross-modal reasoning. The method is therefore a privacy-aware memory-and-retrieval design: share cleaned knowledge, retrieve related cases, and reason without retraining a central model on raw private data.
863.mech: The input is heterogeneous fault data from multiple clients: sensor streams or other modalities that may differ in resolution and type. First, a Resolution-Agnostic Semantic Projector converts each site's signals into semantic vectors. The abstract says this projector uses adaptive spectral pooling, which means it looks at signals in the frequency domain, where repeating patterns are described by their rates rather than by their exact timestamps. That matters for machinery because many faults appear as characteristic vibration or signal frequencies, and different devices may record them at different resolutions. Next, the projected descriptions are passed through Semantic-Shielding. The paper frames this as a privacy step: keep enough information to identify fault meaning while reducing the details an attacker could reverse into the original local sample. Instead of synchronizing model parameters, clients contribute these sanitized lightweight descriptions. The server builds a global knowledge graph from them, connecting related descriptions so rare evidence from one place can become searchable by another place. At diagnosis time, a new fault pattern is projected into the same semantic form. The system retrieves relevant graph evidence and uses a frozen Meta Llama-3.1 model to reason across modalities and produce a fault identification, including zero-shot cases where the local site has not previously observed that fault type.
863.math: Several mathematical ideas are doing specific jobs here. Similarity is the first: each sensor case is compressed into a list of numbers, and the system treats nearby descriptions as related fault evidence. The risk is that closeness may preserve the wrong property, so the projector must make fault-relevant patterns, not private noise or device quirks, define nearness. Spectral analysis is the second idea: a signal can be described by the frequencies it contains, much as a chord can be described by notes rather than by every pressure wave sample. Adaptive spectral pooling keeps frequency information in a way that can tolerate different resolutions. A graph is the third idea: each shared description becomes part of a map, and links let evidence from one client support diagnosis elsewhere. The min-max adversarial game is a controlled contest: one side tries to keep task-useful information, while an opposing side tries to expose private reconstructable information. The Information Bottleneck principle supplies the tradeoff: squeeze the description so it keeps what helps diagnosis and discards what merely reveals the original sample. Retrieval then turns diagnosis into searching a knowledge memory before reasoning.
863.dots: This paper belongs with privacy and federated security papers because it treats sharing itself as a threat surface, not just a plumbing detail. It is close to federated learning work that reduces communication or aligns client knowledge, but it takes a stronger turn by replacing parameter synchronization with shared sanitized knowledge. It also sits inside multimodal learning: the abstract's vibration-like, frequency-aligned signal story has the same deeper problem as vision-language and sensor-language papers, where unlike data types must be placed on a common comparison surface. The RAG connection is also central. Many retrieval-assisted generation papers ask how a language model should use an external memory rather than rely only on what it already knows; here the memory is a privacy-filtered fault graph built across clients. The paper also touches graph reasoning, similarity search, information compression, adversarial privacy, and zero-shot generalization, all recurring conference ideas about moving evidence safely from where it is observed to where it is needed.
863.ww: The mechanism should help because it changes what gets shared. Traditional federated learning shares updates that are tied to model training on local data; rare samples may barely move the shared model, while private details can still leak through the update pattern. Fed-S2 instead shares a cleaned description built for retrieval. That gives rare cases a more direct route into the shared memory: even if a fault appears only a few times, its sanitized description can become a node that another site can retrieve later. Frequency-domain alignment helps because many machine faults are better recognized by recurring signal patterns than by raw sample-by-sample shape, and frequency descriptions can be less tied to a particular sensor resolution. The adversarial bottleneck helps because it makes privacy part of the representation goal rather than an afterthought. Retrieval plus a frozen language model helps zero-shot diagnosis because the model is asked to reason over fetched cross-site evidence, not to have learned every fault through local training examples.
863.po: The payoff claimed in the abstract is large for the setting it targets. On the named cross-domain fault benchmarks CWRU, XJTU-SY, and MFPT, Fed-S2 raises long-tail fault identification from 38.5% to 84.2%. In zero-shot scenarios, where traditional federated learning is reported to fail at 0%, it reaches 68.5% accuracy. The paper also reports a 93% reduction in communication overhead. In practical terms, the promised capability is a privacy-preserving diagnostic memory for smaller infrastructure operators: they can benefit from rare fault evidence observed elsewhere without sending raw data or repeatedly synchronizing heavy model updates.
863.limits: Several assumptions have to hold. The semantic projector must preserve the fault signal that matters while removing private reconstructable detail; if it removes rare diagnostic clues, retrieval will fail. The knowledge graph must connect genuinely related cases rather than artifacts of device type, site, or sensor resolution. The privacy claim depends on the stated adversarial bottleneck and Semantic-Shielding being strong against realistic inversion attacks, but the abstract does not describe the full attacker model. The zero-shot result is grounded in the listed benchmarks, not proof that all future infrastructure faults can be recognized. The frozen Meta Llama-3.1 reasoning step also assumes retrieved evidence is relevant and expressed in a form the model can use reliably.

864.bp: This record is about the Web as a living historical object, not a frozen collection of pages. Pages appear, change, disappear, get archived, are linked from other places, and are later searched by people who care about when something was true. TempWeb serves the community that studies that changing Web. The abstract describes the workshop as a hub for researchers and practitioners who work on infrastructure, scalable methods, and software for aggregating, querying, and analyzing heterogeneous Web data at large scale. The need is practical: a search engine, archive, safety system, or social science study can give the wrong answer if it ignores time. A page about a policy, crisis, product, or person may mean one thing in 2020 and another in 2026. TempWeb's role is to connect the pieces needed to study those changes, from Web archiving and Web mining to temporal information extraction, temporal retrieval, benchmarks, Web evolution, and suicide risk prediction.
864.wh: The hard part is that the temporal Web is not one neat table. It is many kinds of evidence moving at once: pages, links, timestamps, archived snapshots, user posts, search needs, benchmark tasks, and large infrastructure logs. Some evidence is missing because archives do not capture every page at every moment. Some evidence is inconsistent because different sites record time differently. Some evidence is too large to inspect directly because Web-scale collections require methods that save time, memory, and human effort. The meaning of a query also changes when time enters. Asking for information about an event may mean documents before it, documents after it, documents that changed during it, or documents whose language foreshadowed it. The abstract names a broad spectrum, from Web evolution to suicide risk prediction, which shows the central tension: the field needs shared temporal ways of thinking, but the applications have very different data shapes, risks, and evaluation needs.
864.naive: A smart beginner might take the normal Web toolkit and add a date filter. Archive pages, store timestamps, run ordinary search, and group papers under whatever application label they mention. That helps only at the surface. It fails because time is not just an extra column. A page can be absent from an archive even though it existed. A query may need the order of changes, not just one date. A prediction task such as suicide risk depends on a trajectory, not one post. A benchmark must define what is observed, what future is hidden, and how systems are compared. The naive approach treats temporal Web analytics as static Web analytics plus calendar labels, so it misses the deeper problem of how evidence changes and how methods should respect that change.
864.ap: The core idea of this workshop record is coordination around the temporal dimension of the Web. TempWeb is not presented as a single algorithm. It is presented as a recurring research hub that gathers work on the pieces needed to make time a first-class part of Web analysis. In concrete terms, that means bringing together infrastructure for storing and accessing changing Web data, scalable methods for handling large and mixed collections, software for aggregation and querying, and application studies where time changes the answer. The abstract names temporal information extraction and retrieval, Web mining, Web archiving, large-scale data analysis, temporal benchmarks, Web evolution, and suicide risk prediction. The central move is therefore organizational and conceptual: make researchers who might otherwise work separately on archives, search, mining, benchmarks, and health prediction treat their problems as siblings. They are all asking how to recover useful structure from Web evidence whose meaning depends on time.
864.mech: The mechanism, as far as the abstract supports, is a workshop pipeline rather than a model pipeline. The input is a collection of research contributions from academia and industry, spread across core computer science and application scenarios. Each contribution studies some part of the temporal Web: how to collect heterogeneous Web data, how to aggregate it, how to query it, how to analyze it at scale, how to retrieve information with time in mind, how to extract time-related facts from text, how to build or use Web archives, how to design temporal benchmarks, or how to predict an evolving risk signal. TempWeb then acts as the meeting layer. It places these contributions in one venue, so methods built for infrastructure can be seen next to methods built for retrieval, and application problems can reveal where the underlying tools are still weak. The transformation is not a numerical transformation performed by the paper itself. It is a field-level transformation: separate temporal problems are organized into a shared agenda. The output is a connected research conversation and a clearer map of what temporal Web analytics must support. The abstract explicitly says the 16th edition covers the full spectrum from Web evolution through temporal benchmarks to suicide risk prediction, so the mechanism is broad coverage plus repeated community connection.
864.math: The main mathematical idea underneath this record is sequence: the order of observations matters. A Web page snapshot, a user post, or a transaction-like event is not only a fact; it is a fact at a particular moment in a longer path. Sequence reasoning asks what happened before, what changed after, and which gaps make the story uncertain. A second idea is retrieval as choosing a small useful set from a huge pile. Temporal retrieval must decide not only which documents match a need, but which versions or time windows match it. A third idea is information extraction, which means turning text into structured clues such as events, dates, and relations so they can be compared or queried. A fourth idea is systems budgeting: Web-scale analysis must save time, memory, and computation because the raw collection is too large for exhaustive inspection. Finally, prediction under uncertainty appears in the suicide risk example and in neighboring temporal benchmark work in the repo. It asks how repeated earlier signals change belief about later states. The tradeoff running through all of this is completeness versus practicality: keeping every temporal detail would be ideal but often impossible, while compressing time too aggressively destroys the evidence that makes the problem temporal.
864.dots: This paper connects directly to the repo's information retrieval and search family because temporal retrieval is still a ranking problem: from many possible documents or snapshots, the system must return the few that answer a time-sensitive need. It connects to time-series and spatiotemporal work because the Web is treated as a stream of changing observations, not a static store. Neighboring records make that concrete: the FinSurvival Challenge turns time-stamped Web3 events into survival prediction tasks, ANN-TS detects unusual points in high-dimensional Web streams, and the suicide risk paper models a person's online state as a trajectory influenced by posts and comments. TempWeb sits above those examples as connective tissue. It also touches infrastructure and scalability, because archives, benchmarks, and Web-scale analysis cannot succeed if storage and querying are too slow. The broader field-level point is that retrieval, mining, prediction, and archiving all become different faces of the same question once time changes the meaning of evidence.
864.ww: This works as a research agenda because temporal problems often fail at the boundaries between subfields. An archive can preserve pages but still be hard to query by time. A retrieval method can rank documents but ignore that the same page has several historical versions. A prediction method can use posts but miss how social feedback changes across weeks. A benchmark can compare systems but hide the real temporal difficulties if it ignores missing futures or changing behavior. By gathering these strands, TempWeb increases the chance that a method built in one area exposes assumptions useful to another. Infrastructure work tells application researchers what can actually be collected and queried. Application work tells infrastructure researchers which temporal details matter. Benchmarks force vague progress claims into shared tasks. The abstract's hub language is therefore not just decoration; it describes the practical reason the workshop matters. Time-aware Web research needs repeated contact among people studying data collection, search, mining, scale, and domain-specific consequences.
864.po: The payoff is a clearer home for temporal Web analytics at The Web Conference. According to the abstract, the 2026 TempWeb edition connects researchers and practitioners across domains and covers infrastructure, scalable methods, innovative software, temporal information extraction and retrieval, Web mining, Web archiving, large-scale analysis, Web evolution, temporal benchmarks, and suicide risk prediction. For the site's reader, the useful capability is conceptual: TempWeb marks these topics as parts of one shared problem rather than scattered specialties. It helps explain why a benchmark paper, an archive paper, a retrieval paper, and a health-risk prediction paper can belong to the same temporal Web conversation.
864.limits: The abstract is a workshop overview, so it does not prove that one specific method improves accuracy, speed, or reliability. It names areas covered by TempWeb but gives no detailed paper list, experimental setup, benchmark definition, or measured outcome for the workshop itself. The claim that TempWeb is a hub depends on continued participation from researchers and practitioners across the named domains. The technical success of any contribution still depends on its own data quality, time stamps, archive coverage, query design, and evaluation. The abstract supports broad connections across temporal Web topics, but not strong claims about which particular method is best.

865.bp: The paper is about a common problem in work with tables: the raw columns rarely say the useful thing directly. A shop may record clicks, impressions, prices, user groups, and time, but the prediction model may need a derived clue such as a rate, a gap, a grouped count, or a transformed value. Humans traditionally invent these extra columns by knowing the business and trying many candidates. Autonomous feature engineering tries to automate that craft so models can make better predictions without a person hand-building every useful signal. AFE-Master focuses on the moment where language models seem helpful because they can read descriptions and imitate expert reasoning, but where uncontrolled code generation is too messy. The paper's goal is to turn feature construction from open-ended rewriting into a structured search over readable feature recipes, so automatically generated features can be useful, checkable, and transferable from public tabular tasks to a large advertising recommendation service.
865.wh: The hard part is that a feature is not just a string of code. It is a small claim about what relationship in the data might matter. If a system rewrites the whole feature at once, a small intended change can accidentally change its meaning, break an important rule, or make the result impossible to interpret. Traditional autonomous feature engineering can search many combinations, but the abstract says it lacks semantic guidance, meaning it does not have enough understanding of what operations mean in a domain. Language models add language understanding, yet existing approaches often ask them to work in an open code space. That makes edits coarse and non-local: changing one part of a feature may disturb distant parts of the expression. The central tension is therefore search versus control. The system must explore a huge space of possible derived columns, but it must do so through small moves whose meaning and validity can be checked.
865.naive: A smart beginner would ask a language model to write new feature code from the table description, run a model, keep the features that improve prediction, and ask for more rewrites. This might work for a few simple features, but it gives the system almost no handle on the internal structure of each candidate. If a feature fails, the system does not know whether the grouping, transformation, constant, or column choice was wrong. If a feature almost works, rewriting it from scratch can throw away the useful part. The abstract's failure mode is that open code edits are too broad and too tangled, so the search cannot reliably preserve meaning, enforce invariant rules, or build rich hierarchical features.
865.ap: AFE-Master's core move is to give feature construction its own controlled language. Instead of treating a feature as arbitrary program text, it represents the feature as a recipe made from allowed transformations. That recipe is parsed into an abstract syntax tree, which is a tree-shaped breakdown of the expression: operations sit at internal nodes, columns and constants sit near the leaves, and parent-child links show which operation acts on which inputs. This tree gives the language model something structured to inspect and edit. The paper then uses guided local search over nearby syntactic and semantic neighborhoods. In plain terms, it explores small legal changes to the recipe, checks whether those changes still make sense, and keeps moving toward features that carry more predictive information. The shift is from black-box feature evolution to controlled repair and refinement of interpretable feature structures.
865.mech: The input is tabular data, where each row is an example and each column is a measured fact, plus the prediction task and whatever domain description the system can use. AFE-Master first expresses candidate features in a domain-specific language, a restricted vocabulary of valid feature operations rather than unrestricted general code. Each feature expression is parsed into an abstract syntax tree, so the system can see the feature as parts: which raw columns are used, which transformation is applied first, how intermediate values are combined, and what final derived column is produced. The language model works on this structured object instead of freely rewriting a full program. The search then defines neighborhoods around the current feature. A syntactic neighbor may change the shape of the expression by replacing or inserting an allowed operation. A semantic neighbor changes the recipe in a way intended to preserve meaningful constraints, such as keeping operations compatible with the type and meaning of the data. For each small candidate edit, the system can check whether the new feature is valid, add it to a tabular model such as XGBoost, MLP, TabPFN, or the industrial FiBiNET setting described in the abstract, and score whether prediction improves. The output is a set of information-dense, hierarchically structured features that can be inspected as recipes rather than opaque code fragments.
865.math: The main mathematical idea is search over a structured space. The space is all feature recipes allowed by the domain-specific language; each point in that space is one possible derived column. Because the number of recipes is enormous, the system cannot test everything. Local search means starting from a current recipe, looking at nearby recipes made by small edits, scoring them, and moving toward better ones. The score is tied to prediction quality: a feature is useful if a model trained with it makes fewer mistakes or earns better task outcomes. The tree representation supplies discrete structure. A tree is useful because it preserves composition: one operation can feed another, so the system knows exactly which part of the recipe a change touches. The language model contributes a learned prior, meaning a tendency to suggest edits that look semantically plausible from domain and code patterns it has seen before. The domain-specific language supplies constraints, which are mathematical boundaries on the search: only valid operations and valid combinations are allowed. The central tradeoff is exploration versus control. A completely free search may discover surprising features but can break meaning; a tightly constrained search may be safer but miss useful ideas. AFE-Master tries to keep both by letting small, checkable moves explore a meaningful feature space.
865.dots: This paper sits in the conference's broader optimization thread: when the possible choices are too many to enumerate, define what counts as better, make a candidate move, measure the result, and repeat. It connects to recommendation and advertising papers because features are often the hidden machinery behind ranking decisions; better derived columns can help a model decide which item, ad, or user response is more likely. It also connects to language-model systems that use structure to keep model behavior grounded. Graph-enhanced language-model work uses explicit relationships to reduce unsupported answers; AFE-Master uses a formal feature language and trees to reduce unsupported code edits. The paper also belongs with interpretability work because it refuses to treat predictive gain as enough. A generated feature has to be readable as a hierarchy of operations, so a practitioner can inspect what raw facts were combined and why the resulting signal might make sense.
865.ww: The mechanism should improve over the naive approach because it preserves useful partial work. If a generated feature is almost right, the tree tells the system where it can make a small change instead of replacing the whole expression. That makes learning from feedback easier: a good score can be attached to a recipe and its nearby variants, while a bad score can rule out a particular operation or combination. The domain-specific language also prevents many pointless candidates before they waste evaluation time. Because every feature is built from known operations, the system can enforce invariant constraints and avoid edits that produce invalid or meaningless columns. The language model is most useful when it is steering this structured search, not when it is asked to write unbounded code. Its semantic knowledge can suggest promising neighborhoods, while the local search and model evaluation decide whether the suggestion actually helps prediction. This explains why the abstract emphasizes both control and practical value: the method gains from language understanding without surrendering the search to arbitrary generation.
865.po: The payoff is a more practical form of automatic feature engineering for tabular prediction. In the abstract, AFE-Master is tested on Kaggle and OpenML tasks, across multiple tabular models including XGBoost, MLP, and TabPFN. It is also tested in a large online advertising recommendation service: 20 automatically generated features are added to an already mature set of 167 expert-crafted features, and the abstract reports gains in CPM and CTR on more than 100 million live samples. The important capability is not just higher scores. It is the ability to discover features that are information-rich, structured, and inspectable enough to be used in serious production settings.
865.limits: The claims depend on the domain-specific language being expressive enough to contain useful features and restrictive enough to block bad ones. If the best feature requires an operation outside the language, the search may never find it. If the language model's suggestions are poorly matched to the domain, local search may spend effort in unhelpful neighborhoods. The abstract reports strong experiments, including a large online test, but it does not prove that the same feature language or search guidance will work equally well for every table, target, or industry. The method also still relies on evaluation feedback from trained models, so noisy, delayed, biased, or expensive feedback can mislead the search.

866.bp: A search system is often asked to pick a small set of documents from a very large collection. The user supplies a query, and the system must quickly decide which documents deserve to be inspected, shown, or passed to a later answer system. Dense retrieval does this by turning the query and each document into compact numerical descriptions, then comparing those descriptions for closeness. That makes search fast and powerful, but it also hides the reason for a match. If a document rises in the list, a human may not know whether the model found the passage that truly answers the query or merely reacted to some surface wording. This paper serves systems where retrieval must be both useful and trustworthy: the ranking should change when the real answer-bearing passage changes, and should stay mostly steady when irrelevant text is edited. The central goal is not only better ranking, but a model whose sensitivity points to the text that actually matters.
866.wh: The hard part is that a document is not relevant as one solid block. A long document may contain one passage that answers the query, many passages that are background, and other passages that share tempting words without helping. A retrieval model that compresses the whole document into one comparison object can blur these roles together. An attacker can exploit that blur by adding or changing text that looks useful to the model while not making the document genuinely more relevant. Explainability fails for the same reason: if the score comes from a mixed document-level signal, it is difficult to say which passage caused the ranking. The paper defines a stricter behavior. When a key relevance passage is changed, the model's output should vary strongly. When an irrelevant passage is changed, the output should vary weakly. That is difficult because the method is unsupervised, so it cannot rely on a large set of human passage labels that say exactly which words caused relevance.
866.naive: A smart beginner might train a dense retriever on query-document pairs, then trust the highest similarity score. If the query and document descriptions are close, the document is treated as relevant; if they are far, it is ignored. This works as a first filter, but it does not ask why the document was close. Another beginner fix would be to perturb random passages and see whether the score changes. That also falls short, because random changes do not distinguish answer-bearing passages from decorative or off-topic passages. The model may learn to be stable everywhere, which hides real evidence, or unstable everywhere, which makes it easy to fool. The missing piece is a disciplined comparison between changes that should matter and changes that should not.
866.ap: The core idea is to train the retriever around counterfactual passages: altered versions of document passages that ask, in effect, what would the score have been if this part of the document were different. The paper wants the model to behave like a careful reader. If the paragraph that makes the document relevant is removed or changed, the reader's belief should move. If a side paragraph is edited, the belief should not move much. The method uses counterfactual regularization, meaning an added training pressure that rewards this pattern of sensitivity. It also draws on game theory by treating passages like contributors to a shared outcome: the document's relevance to a query. A passage receives importance when changing it changes the outcome. The contrastive part is learning by comparison: altered relevant and irrelevant passages create examples that should be separated by their effect on the retrieval score, even without direct human labels.
866.mech: The mechanism starts with a query, a document, and passage-level pieces of that document. The retriever produces a score or ordering signal that says how well the document matches the query. Instead of stopping there, the training process creates counterfactual versions of the document by modifying passages. Some modifications target passages that appear to determine relevance; others affect passages that should not determine relevance. For each altered version, the model observes how much the retrieval output changes. The desired pattern is asymmetric. Changing an important passage should create high variance: the score or ranking signal should move because the evidence has changed. Changing an unimportant passage should create low variance: the document should not be promoted or demoted merely because irrelevant text was touched. The game-theoretic part gives a way to think about passage contribution. If the whole document's relevance is the group outcome, each passage can be judged by how the outcome changes when that passage is present, absent, or altered. The unsupervised learning part matters because the abstract does not claim human annotations for key passages. Instead, the model learns from constructed comparisons among original and counterfactual passages. The output is still a dense retrieval model, but one trained to rank documents while also revealing which passage-level changes explain its ranking behavior.
866.math: The first mathematical idea is similarity: the query and document are converted into compact numerical descriptions so closeness can stand in for relevance. This is useful because a large collection can be searched by comparing numbers, but it is risky because one number-like comparison can hide which part of a document mattered. The second idea is counterfactual reasoning: compare the observed document with a nearby imagined version where one passage has been changed. If the retrieval score changes, that passage had evidence the model cared about; if the score barely changes, it probably was not driving relevance. The third idea is learning by comparison, often called contrastive learning, where the model is trained by seeing pairs or groups that should behave differently. Here the important comparison is not simply relevant versus irrelevant document, but relevant-passage change versus irrelevant-passage change. The fourth idea is game-theoretic contribution: when several passages jointly produce a document score, importance can be estimated by asking how much each passage changes the shared outcome. The tradeoff is sensitivity versus stability. A good retriever must be sensitive enough to notice real relevance evidence, but stable enough that irrelevant edits and adversarial padding do not swing the ranking.
866.dots: This paper sits in the retrieval and search family because it tackles the repeated conference problem of choosing a small useful set from a huge candidate pool. It connects to ranking because the practical decision is an order: which documents rise high enough to be seen. It connects to similarity because dense retrieval depends on learned closeness between a query and a document. It connects to causality because the paper asks which passage actually caused the score to change, rather than merely co-occurred with words from the query. It also connects to explainability and adversarial robustness: the same passage-level sensitivity that exposes why a document matched also makes it harder to promote a document through irrelevant edits. Neighboring work on retrieval-augmented generation, dense retrieval compression, and search security faces the same pressure. Search systems are no longer judged only by whether they retrieve something plausible; they must retrieve evidence that can survive inspection, attacks, and downstream use.
866.ww: The method should work better than the naive approach because it trains the model on the specific failure a naive dense retriever ignores. A normal retriever can be rewarded for placing a document near a query even if it used the wrong part of the document to do so. Counterfactual passage changes make that hidden mistake visible. If the model reacts strongly when irrelevant text is edited, training can push it toward stability on that kind of change. If it barely reacts when the key passage is edited, training can push it toward greater dependence on the true relevance signal. Over many such comparisons, the model is encouraged to put its trust in passages whose alteration changes the document's actual relation to the query. That also explains the adversarial benefit. An attacker trying to add promotional or misleading text without adding real relevance should mostly be changing irrelevant passages. A model trained to keep low variance under those changes has less reason to move the document upward.
866.po: The payoff is a dense retrieval model that is useful in two ways at once. First, it should be more resistant to attacks that try to promote documents without making them genuinely relevant to the query. Second, it gives a path toward explanation, because the model's score changes can indicate which passages were actually responsible for relevance. The abstract also grounds the contribution in an unsupervised setting, which matters because passage-level relevance labels are expensive and often unavailable. The result is not described as a new user interface or a complete security guarantee; it is a training approach for making an existing class of retrieval models more sensitive to the right evidence.
866.limits: The abstract is thin after introducing the cooperative game, so several details are not visible here: how counterfactual passages are generated, how important passages are initially identified, what attacks are tested, and how explanation quality is measured. The approach assumes that altering a key passage should change the retrieval score and altering an irrelevant passage should not, which is reasonable but can break when relevance is spread across many small clues. It also assumes counterfactual edits are realistic enough to teach the right sensitivity. If the generated changes are unnatural, the model may learn artifacts of the editing process. Finally, robustness here means resistance to the described promotion-style attacks, not proof against every adversarial strategy.

867.bp: Many important decisions depend on linked facts rather than rows in a simple table. In healthcare, a patient may have diseases, treatments, symptoms, lab results, and medical categories connected by many kinds of relationships. In economics or industrial production, companies, machines, materials, failures, prices, and policies can be connected in similar webs. This paper asks how to reason about causes inside that kind of web. The practical need is not just to predict that two things often appear together. A decision maker wants to ask what would happen if one thing changed: if a treatment were given, if a part were replaced, or if a policy were altered. The abstract says ordinary causal tools mostly expect flat, fully observed, independent records. Knowledge graphs violate that picture. They include different kinds of entities, labeled relationships, background ontologies, logical rules, and missing facts. The thesis tries to make causal discovery, inference, and counterfactual prediction work directly over those structured fact webs.
867.wh: The difficulty starts with the shape of the evidence. A flat table treats each record as a separate case with a fixed set of columns. A knowledge graph is more like a map: one fact points to another, relationship labels have meanings, and some facts are absent simply because nobody has recorded them yet. The abstract names three central breaks. First, semantic unawareness can cause inaccurate estimation. If the method ignores what relation types, categories, and logical constraints mean, it may compare things that only look alike at the surface. Second, incompleteness violates causal assumptions. Under the open world assumption, a missing link is not proof that the link is false, so absence is dangerous evidence. Third, relational dependencies create interference between entities. One entity's state or action can affect another through graph links, so cases are not cleanly independent. A causal estimate is hard because the comparison group, the missing facts, and the route of influence are all shaped by graph structure.
867.naive: A smart beginner might flatten the graph into a table. For each entity, they would count nearby relation types, mark whether certain attributes are present, and then run a standard causal method as if each entity were an independent row. That feels reasonable because many causal tools need table-shaped input. It fails because the flattening throws away the meaning of the links and rules. A missing fact may be treated as false. Two entities connected by a path may be treated as separate observations even when influence can pass between them. Ontological information, such as one category implying another, may never enter the estimate. The result can look mathematically clean while answering the wrong causal question.
867.ap: The paper's central move is to bring causal reasoning and knowledge representation into the same machinery instead of translating one into a damaged version of the other. The abstract describes a series of semantics-aware frameworks: CauseKG, SemMatch, HyKG-CF, and BaLu. The shared idea is that causal questions over a knowledge graph should respect the graph's own language. Entities are not just anonymous rows; relation labels, ontological categories, logical entailments, and linked neighborhoods help define what can cause what, what evidence is comparable, and what facts may be missing. The approach therefore treats causal discovery, causal inference, and counterfactual prediction as graph-native tasks. It uses formal modeling and query-based reasoning so a user can ask causal questions directly over the graph rather than first destroying the graph's structure. In concrete terms, the system tries to learn causal knowledge, represent it with the semantics of the graph, and reason over it while accounting for incompleteness and relational dependence.
867.mech: The input is a knowledge graph: a collection of entities connected by typed relations, enriched with ontological meanings and logical constraints. The first job is to read the graph as more than a pile of edges. Relation types say what kind of connection exists. Ontological semantics say how entity categories and relation meanings fit together. Logical entailment says that some facts can be inferred from other facts, so the system should not rely only on explicitly written edges. From there, the proposed pipeline learns causal knowledge, meaning it tries to identify which connected pieces are possible drivers of change rather than mere companions. CauseKG, SemMatch, HyKG-CF, and BaLu are named in the abstract as parts of this line of work, together covering discovery, inference, counterfactual prediction, formal modeling, and query-based reasoning. A causal discovery step asks what cause-effect structure is plausible in the graph. A causal inference step estimates what change would follow from an intervention while respecting graph semantics and dependencies. A counterfactual step asks what would have been predicted if some condition or link had differed. Query-based reasoning then turns these learned or modeled structures into answers to user questions. The output is not just a score; it is causal intelligence over the graph: discovered causal relations, estimated effects, and counterfactual answers that are meant to remain interpretable because they are tied to graph semantics and logical structure.
867.math: The main mathematical idea is causal comparison under structure. Causality asks about two worlds: the one observed and another one where a chosen action or condition changed. Only one world is directly seen, so the missing comparison has to be estimated from evidence. In ordinary table settings, the method often assumes that records are fully described and independent enough to compare. This paper's setting breaks both assumptions. Graph mathematics enters because the evidence is made of nodes and links. Nodes are entities; links are typed relations; paths can carry possible influence or explanation. Logical reasoning enters because some facts are not listed directly but follow from ontologies and constraints. Under the open world assumption, absence is uncertain rather than false, so probability-like caution is needed when drawing conclusions from missing links. Interference is another causal idea: if linked entities can affect one another, changing one case may alter its neighbors, so the unit being compared is not isolated. The mathematical tradeoff is actionability versus assumption. A causal answer is useful because it supports decisions, but it is trustworthy only if the graph semantics, inferred facts, dependency structure, and missing-data treatment describe the real system closely enough. The paper's semantics-aware framing exists because the same numeric estimate can mean different things depending on what the graph relation actually says.
867.dots: This paper sits at the crossing of the repo's causal-inference and knowledge-graph families. The causal-inference family is about repairing broken comparisons: separating a real driver from a coincidence when the missing alternative world cannot be observed. The knowledge-graph family is about using linked evidence without pretending that all links are equally reliable or complete. This thesis combines both pressures. It also connects to graph learning, because neighbors and relation paths can carry evidence but can also spread misleading signals. It connects to retrieval-augmented and question-answering work over graphs, where query-based reasoning depends on whether the graph contains the right paths and constraints. The abstract names healthcare, economics, and industrial production, which places the work near decision-support systems where a wrong causal claim can lead to a wrong action, not merely a wrong label. Compared with papers that use graphs for prediction alone, this one asks a stricter question: what would change if part of the graph-described world were changed?
867.ww: The approach should improve over the naive table conversion because it keeps the information that defines the causal question. If relation labels and ontological categories are meaningful, then two graph neighborhoods with similar surface shapes may still describe different real situations. A semantics-aware method can avoid comparing them as if they were interchangeable. Logical entailment helps because a graph can imply facts that are not explicitly written; using those implied facts can reduce the damage caused by incompleteness. Treating the open world assumption seriously also prevents a common mistake: reading an unobserved link as evidence that no relationship exists. Accounting for relational dependencies matters because influence may travel through links. If one entity's outcome depends on another, the method should not count them as independent pieces of evidence. The end-to-end pipeline works in principle because discovery, modeling, inference, counterfactual prediction, and querying are aligned around the same structured representation. Instead of learning a cause in one simplified form and answering in another, the causal claim remains attached to entities, relation types, rules, and graph paths that a human can inspect.
867.po: The payoff is a way to ask causal questions directly over knowledge graphs. According to the abstract, the thesis establishes an end-to-end pipeline that unifies causal knowledge learning, formal modeling, and query-based reasoning. That buys three capabilities: finding plausible causal structure in a graph, estimating cause-effect relationships while respecting semantics, and predicting counterfactual outcomes over graph-described entities. The practical value is strongest in domains where decisions depend on connected records and background meaning, such as healthcare, economics, and industrial production. The claimed benefit is trustworthy and interpretable causal intelligence, meaning answers that are not only numerical predictions but are tied to the graph's relations, constraints, and reasoning paths.
867.limits: The abstract supports the design goal and named components, but it does not give datasets, metrics, baselines, or deployment evidence in the provided input. The approach assumes the knowledge graph's ontology, relation labels, and logical constraints are accurate enough to guide causal reasoning. If the graph encodes biased, stale, or mistaken facts, semantics-aware reasoning can faithfully preserve those mistakes. The method also depends on missing data being handled well under the open world assumption; severe incompleteness may still hide the crucial cause. Relational interference must match real influence rather than mere connection. The abstract does not prove that the pipeline transfers across all graph domains, graph sizes, causal query types, or high-stakes decisions.

868.bp: Peer review is one of the control points in research: a submitted paper is judged by people who are expected to read it carefully, explain strengths and weaknesses, and avoid claims that are not actually supported by the paper. At conference scale, that control point becomes hard to watch. Editors and program chairs may receive many reviews, each written in free text, with different styles and levels of care. This paper asks whether large language models, meaning text systems trained to predict and interpret language, can help audit that process. The task is not to replace reviewers. The useful system is more like a second reader that checks two practical questions: is this review specific and professionally toned, and are its factual claims grounded in the submitted work? The abstract matters because research integrity depends not only on catching fake papers or bad citations, but also on checking whether the gatekeeping conversation itself is careful and evidence based.
868.wh: The hard part is that a review can be bad in ways that are subtle. A short review may be shallow, but length alone is not quality. A review can sound confident while making a claim the paper never supports. A review can be polite but vague, or detailed but unfairly harsh. The system must therefore judge both language behavior and evidence behavior. For quality, it needs to recognize specificity, tone, and alignment with human judgment. For factual grounding, it must compare a reviewer sentence against the submitted paper and decide whether the paper actually backs it. That is harder than ordinary text classification because the answer depends on two documents and on expert norms. It is also harder than asking a language model directly, because fluent explanations can hide unsupported reasoning. The abstract says the authors compare simple fixed measurements, machine-learning baselines, direct language-model use, and models adapted to the task because no single signal is obviously enough.
868.naive: A smart beginner would start with easy measurements: count review length, count concrete-looking words, flag rude phrases, and maybe ask a language model, without examples, to score the review. This would catch some obvious problems. Very short, generic, or openly hostile reviews often leave visible traces. But it fails where integrity actually becomes difficult. A long review can still avoid the paper's substance. A claim can be phrased calmly while being unsupported. A language model may reward a review that sounds expert even if it invented what the paper said. The beginner method also treats review quality and factual grounding as the same problem, when one asks about the usefulness of feedback and the other asks whether a claim has evidence in a separate submitted document.
868.ap: The central move is to treat peer-review auditing as two connected but different checks, then evaluate which kinds of automated systems align with expert human judgments. One system assesses review quality along dimensions named in the abstract, such as specificity and tone. Another system verifies factual grounding: it asks whether claims made by a reviewer are supported by the paper under review. The paper does not present the language model as magic. It compares several levels of machinery. Static metrics are fixed measurements such as surface features. Machine-learning baselines are trained pattern recognizers that learn from labeled examples. Direct language-model use asks a general model to perform the task without task-specific training. Adapted models are adjusted on examples from this setting. The important design choice is the hybrid conclusion: the abstract reports that interpretable machine learning and evidence search can be more reliable than relying on a language model alone.
868.mech: The mechanism begins with two texts that normally live together in peer review: the submitted paper and the review written about it. For the quality-audit task, the review is the main input. The system turns it into signals related to dimensions such as specificity and tone. Specificity means whether the review points to concrete parts of the work rather than giving generic praise or criticism. Tone means whether the language is constructive, dismissive, hostile, or otherwise misaligned with review norms. Different candidate systems produce scores or labels for these dimensions, and those outputs are compared with expert annotations, meaning judgments supplied by people who know what good reviewing looks like. For factual grounding, the input is a reviewer claim plus the submitted paper. The system must find relevant parts of the paper, compare them with the claim, and decide whether the claim is supported. A claim like a statement about a method, result, dataset, or limitation should not pass merely because it sounds plausible. The comparison pipeline therefore needs a search step that brings likely evidence into view, a matching step that checks whether the evidence says the same thing, and an output that can be audited by humans. The deployment setting adds another layer: at scale, the system must route many reviews through these checks consistently, while preserving enough interpretability that editors can see why something was flagged.
868.math: The main mathematical idea is scoring under uncertainty. A review is not simply good or bad by one obvious property, so the system defines measurable targets: specificity, tone, and support for claims. Each target becomes a question whose answer can be compared with expert labels. Static metrics use counting and rule-like measurement: how much text is present, what words or patterns appear, and whether simple features correlate with expert judgment. Trained machine-learning baselines use examples: if past reviews with human labels show that certain language patterns often signal specificity or poor tone, the model reuses those patterns on new reviews. Large language models add a broader learned sense of language, but that learned sense is still a prediction from patterns, not direct proof. Fine-tuning, meaning adjusting a model on task-specific examples, tries to move the model's scoring closer to this review-auditing setting. For factual grounding, the key math is similarity and ranking: parts of the submitted paper are ordered by how likely they are to support a claim. Then a comparison is made between the claim and the retrieved evidence. The tradeoff is breadth versus trust. A broader language model sees many linguistic cues, but a narrower interpretable or evidence-search system may make fewer unsupported leaps because it exposes the text used for the decision.
868.dots: This paper sits beside several recurring conference ideas, but in a research-integrity setting. It connects to retrieval-augmented systems because the factual-grounding task requires finding relevant evidence in the submitted paper before judging a reviewer claim. It connects to language-model evaluation because the authors compare direct use of large language models with adapted models and simpler baselines, asking when fluent text understanding matches expert judgment. It also connects to explainability and trustworthy Web data management: a deployed audit system cannot merely announce that a review is low quality; it must provide a reason that an editor can inspect. Neighboring papers in the same batch show similar pressures from other directions. The robust dense retrieval paper worries about whether a retrieval model reacts to the truly relevant passage rather than irrelevant changes. The graph-enhanced language-model workshop worries about grounding and accountability. This paper brings the same deeper question into scholarly governance: when should an automated text system be trusted as a checker of human-written claims?
868.ww: The approach works when it separates tasks that look similar on the surface but require different evidence. Review quality can often be judged from the review itself: vague language, lack of concrete references, or problematic tone are visible in the review text. Factual grounding cannot be judged that way, because the support lives in the submitted paper. A language model alone may blur these two cases, using general plausibility as if it were proof. Adding retrieval, meaning searching the paper for relevant passages, changes the decision from a free-floating opinion into a comparison between a claim and source text. Comparing system outputs with expert-annotated examples also keeps the target anchored: the question becomes not whether the machine sounds reasonable, but whether it agrees with trained human judgment on the dimensions being measured. Hybrid approaches can win because they combine complementary strengths. Language models can interpret varied phrasing and tone. Interpretable models and retrieval can expose simple signals and concrete evidence. Together they reduce the two main naive failures: mistaking polish for quality and mistaking plausibility for support.
868.po: The payoff is an infrastructure idea for research integrity at scale. Editors, chairs, or platform operators could use such systems to surface reviews that are vague, poorly toned, or factually unsupported, then send the flagged cases to humans for closer inspection. The abstract reports that the authors built and deployed two real-world systems, so the contribution is not only a lab comparison. It also includes deployment lessons and empirical insight into where language models help and where hybrid methods are more dependable. The immediate capability is review auditing; the broader payoff is making the peer-review process easier to monitor without pretending that automated checks can replace expert judgment.
868.limits: The abstract does not prove that language models can uphold research integrity on their own. It explicitly emphasizes capabilities and limitations, and says hybrid approaches with interpretable machine learning and retrieval perform more reliably in some places. The systems depend on expert-annotated evaluation data; if those labels are narrow, inconsistent, or tied to one venue's norms, the audit may not transfer. Factual grounding also assumes the submitted paper contains clear evidence that can be found and compared. Some reviewer judgments are interpretive rather than factual, so support may be partial or debatable. Deployment creates further assumptions about privacy, author trust, reviewer behavior, and how humans act on flags.

869.bp: Many real systems are watched as several measurements changing over time: a medical signal, a factory reading, a traffic trace, a market indicator, or any collection of variables recorded step after step. The practical question is not only what will happen next. It is which earlier movement helps explain a later movement in another variable. That is the Granger causal discovery task: if the past of one series helps predict the future of another beyond what the second series already tells us, the first may be treated as a useful cause-like driver in the recorded system. This paper serves that setting when raw numbers alone are too thin. A time series may contain the rhythm of change, but not the ordinary meaning of what the variables are, what domain they come from, or which relationships are plausible. LLM-GC tries to add that missing contextual layer by bringing language-model world knowledge into causal discovery over time.
869.wh: The hard part is that time series can look related for several reasons that are not useful causes. Two variables may rise together because both follow a shared season, because the data are short and noisy, or because a flexible neural model memorizes accidental wiggles. Existing neural Granger methods can model nonlinear dependencies, meaning they can follow relationships that are not simple straight-line changes, but the abstract says they are confined to raw time-series data. That confinement matters. Raw values say that variable A moved before variable B, but they do not say what A and B mean, whether the direction is physically or socially plausible, or whether a pattern is a repeated mechanism rather than a local accident. Adding language knowledge also creates its own difficulty: contextual information must help the time evidence without being mixed into it so carelessly that the model invents cross-modality causal entanglement.
869.naive: A smart beginner would feed the recorded variables into a neural Granger model and ask it to learn which past values best predict future values. If variable A's past repeatedly improves prediction for variable B, draw an arrow from A to B. That can work when the data are plentiful, clean, and self-explanatory. It fails when the numbers do not carry enough meaning by themselves. The model may learn a coincidence that appears in the training records, mistake a shared background pattern for a directional link, or overfit, which here means fitting temporary quirks rather than a stable relation. The beginner might then append text descriptions, but simply mixing text and numbers can blur which source supports which causal claim.
869.ap: The paper's central move is to treat causal discovery as a two-source evidence problem. One source is temporal: the ordered measurements and their changing dependencies. The other source is contextual: semantic priors and world knowledge distilled from large language models, meaning language systems used here as stores of broad textual associations. LLM-GC does not just paste these together. It uses dual-modality encoding so the numerical stream and the contextual description each get their own representation. Then Cross-Modal Dual Retrieval is used to capture and align temporal and contextual dynamics while avoiding causal entanglement across modalities. The core bet is that a causal pattern should be stronger when the time evidence and contextual evidence point to consistent structure. The paper then uses a causality-aware attention mechanism, made by inverting the conventional attention structure, so a shared augmenter can highlight causal patterns that remain consistent across the two sources.
869.mech: The input is a multivariate time series plus contextual information that can be turned into semantic guidance by a large language model. First, the temporal side is encoded so the system has a compact description of how each variable moves over time and how past values may relate to later values. Separately, the contextual side is encoded so the system has a compact description of what the variables and setting mean in ordinary or domain language. Second, Cross-Modal Dual Retrieval searches across these two sources in both directions: temporal evidence can retrieve relevant contextual clues, and contextual clues can retrieve relevant temporal patterns. This is meant to align the two views without declaring every cross-view match to be causal. Third, the system extracts multimodal causal features. The abstract says it does this with a causality-aware self-attention mechanism formed by inverting the conventional structure. In plain terms, attention is a scoring rule that decides which pieces should listen to which other pieces; here the scoring is reorganized so causal consistency is emphasized rather than general association. Finally, a shared causality augmenter strengthens patterns that appear consistently across the temporal and contextual views, and the output is a discovered Granger causal structure among the time-series variables.
869.math: The first mathematical idea is Granger causality, which is a prediction-based test for directional usefulness in time. It asks whether knowing the past of one variable reduces uncertainty about another variable's future after the target variable's own past has already been considered. This is weaker than proving physical cause, but useful because time gives a natural order: causes must appear before the changes they help explain. The second idea is representation learning, meaning converting raw values or text into compact descriptions that preserve useful differences. The tradeoff is compression versus detail: the description must forget accidental noise but keep signal relevant to causal discovery. The third idea is retrieval, which means comparing a current representation against a collection of candidates and bringing back the closest useful evidence. Here retrieval crosses modalities, so numerical patterns and semantic clues can inform each other. The fourth idea is attention, a learned weighting scheme that assigns more influence to selected pieces of evidence. The paper changes that structure to be causality-aware, so the weights are meant to emphasize stable driver-response patterns instead of any strong correlation. Underneath all of this is optimization: the model chooses internal settings that reduce wrong causal predictions on the training task.
869.dots: This paper sits at the intersection of the repo's causal-inference and time-series/spatiotemporal families. Like other causal papers, it is trying to repair a broken comparison: which earlier factor helps explain a later outcome, rather than merely moving beside it. Like other time-series papers, it must preserve order, rhythm, and dependency structure before making a decision. It also connects to graph learning because the final causal discovery can be read as a directed graph whose nodes are variables and whose links are proposed driver-response relations. It connects to language-model papers because it uses a large language model not as the final answerer, but as a source of semantic priors. The neighboring CACGL-style problem in the repo asks about hidden causes and changing relationships in multivariate time series; LLM-GC instead emphasizes missing context and overfitting when causal discovery looks only at raw numeric traces.
869.ww: The mechanism should help because it attacks two different failure modes at once. Raw temporal evidence is necessary: without ordered measurements, Granger discovery has no basis for saying one variable's past helps another variable's future. But raw evidence can be brittle when the series is short, noisy, or full of accidental associations. Contextual semantics can act as a soft guardrail by saying which relationships are plausible in the world described by the variables. At the same time, context alone is not enough, because language-model knowledge can be vague, biased, or mismatched to the actual data. LLM-GC therefore asks the two views to meet through retrieval and alignment. A pattern that is strong only in the numbers may be an overfit coincidence; a pattern that is only suggested by text may be unsupported by the observed sequence. A pattern that survives both views is more likely to be a stable causal candidate. The shared causality augmenter then concentrates model capacity on those cross-view consistencies rather than letting each modality produce separate, conflicting causal stories.
869.po: The payoff is a causal discovery system for time series that is less trapped inside raw numeric traces. According to the abstract, LLM-GC is the first approach to bridge large language models and Granger causality, and it is evaluated on both synthetic and real-world benchmark datasets. Its practical gain is not just a higher score. It gives the model a way to use temporal dynamics and contextual meaning together, so causal links can be chosen with more information than past values alone provide. The reported result is that LLM-GC outperforms existing neural Granger causal discovery methods in those evaluations.
869.limits: The abstract does not prove that the discovered links are true physical causes; Granger causality remains a prediction-based notion of directional usefulness. The method also assumes that language-model semantic priors are relevant to the variables being studied and do not inject misleading world knowledge. Cross-modal retrieval must align the right contextual clues with the right temporal patterns, or it may reinforce a plausible but false story. The promised avoidance of causal entanglement across modalities depends on the design working as intended. The experiments cover synthetic and real-world benchmark datasets, but the abstract does not establish transfer to every domain, long time horizon, noisy sensor setting, or case with important unobserved causes.
